orient: In the first edition of 1847, the novel filled two volumes, and Volume II begins here. Lockwood opens the chapter a week later in his diary (winter 1801–02), still recovering, and says he will tell the rest of Nelly's story in her own words. Then Nelly takes up the tale again, a few days after her visit to the Heights in Chapter XIV, in March 1784.

notes.t: so many days nearer health, and spring
notes.g: Lockwood is recovering, and winter is passing.
notes.n: He fell ill after his night at the Heights in Chapter III and has been in bed ever since.

notes.g: The story of Heathcliff, his neighbour and landlord.
Nelly Dean, housekeeper at the Grange.

notes.m: 'Fair' here means good, capable, not 'just' or 'pale'.

notes.t: the evening of my visit to the Heights
notes.g: The day of Nelly's visit in Chapter XIV, when Heathcliff forced her to carry his letter.

notes.t: Mr. Heathcliff was about the place
notes.g: Heathcliff was hanging around the Grange.

notes.m: Stronger than playful teasing: worried and bullied.
Not a slip of paper for a purchase: the act of getting the letter.

notes.t: after the family were gone to church
notes.g: After the household had left for Sunday church.
notes.n: Masters and most servants went to church on Sunday morning, so the house was nearly empty.

notes.t: a man servant left to keep the house
notes.g: A male servant left behind to look after the house.
The time of the church service.

notes.m: 'Engagement' means an agreement or promise, not a betrothal.

notes.g: The lady of the house: Catherine.
Imported fruit, a treat for an invalid.
notes.n: Oranges came by sea from Spain and Portugal and were a luxury, especially in a remote country village. A clever excuse to send the servant far off.

notes.t: to be paid for on the morrow
notes.g: To be paid for the next day.
notes.n: He could not pay on a Sunday; shops would give a known household credit.

notes.g: A thin wrap worn round the shoulders.

notes.t: Her thick, long hair had been partly removed
notes.g: Some of her hair had been cut off.
notes.n: Cutting a fever patient's hair was a standard treatment, believed to cool the head and calm the brain.

notes.g: As she put weight back on.
Painfully reminding you of what caused them.

notes.t: the touching interest which she awakened
notes.g: The tender sympathy she stirred in others.

notes.t: refuted more tangible proofs of convalescence
notes.g: Contradicted the more solid signs that she was recovering.
notes.n: 'Convalescence' is the period of getting better after illness.

notes.t: stamped her as one doomed to decay
notes.g: Marked her out as someone fated to waste away.

notes.m: 'Divert' here means entertain, as in 'diversion', not 'redirect'.

notes.g: Activity; something to keep busy with.
The church in the nearby village of Gimmerton.
notes.n: Lockwood dreamt about this chapel in Chapter III. A 'chapel' here is a small local church.
'Beck' is the northern word for a brook.

notes.g: The summer leaves on the trees.

notes.t: which drowned that music about the Grange
notes.g: Which drowned out the sound of the stream near the Grange.
A big melting of snow and ice.

notes.n: There were no envelopes then: a letter was folded and closed with a blob of wax, the 'seal'.

notes.m: 'Peruse' means to read thoroughly, not to skim.

notes.g: Someone to explain it to her.

notes.t: the open house was too tempting
notes.g: The doors standing open were too great a temptation.

notes.m: A time word, not 'in a straight line'.

notes.g: No hope she would recover in the end.
Heathcliff's name for Catherine, from their childhood.

notes.t: her humour was a mere vane for constantly varying caprices
notes.g: Her mood swung like a weathervane with every whim.
notes.m: 'Humour' means mood, not comedy. 'Caprices' are sudden whims.

notes.g: Done well out of it; flourished.

notes.t: when I am in the earth
That’s the grave of Catherine Earnshaw?
notes.g: Catherine imagines Heathcliff at her grave years from now.
notes.n: She calls herself by her maiden name, Earnshaw, not her married name, Linton. Remember the names scratched on the window ledge in Chapter III.

notes.t: my children are dearer to me
notes.g: My children are more precious to me.

notes.t: heaven would be a land of exile to her
notes.g: Heaven would feel like banishment to her.
notes.n: In Chapter IX Catherine told Nelly she dreamt heaven did not seem to be her home, and she wept to come back to earth.

notes.t: unless with her mortal body she cast away her moral character also
notes.g: Unless she left her nature behind along with her body.

notes.t: inadequate was his stock of gentleness

notes.g: Four clear blue bruises from his fingers.
Taken over by an evil spirit.
notes.n: Biblical language: in the Gospels Jesus casts devils out of people 'possessed with devils'.

notes.g: Burnt into my memory, like a brand on cattle.

notes.t: writhe in the torments of hell
notes.g: Twist in agony as if in hell.
The sudden violent attack (of her heart).
In the future; after I'm gone.
If you keep your anger alive.
Pale and discoloured with strong feeling.
notes.m: 'Livid' originally meant leaden, bluish-grey, not simply 'furious'.

notes.n: 'Accents' here means tone of voice.
An old religious idea: the soul is trapped in the body as in a prison, and freed at death.
In northern and Scottish speech, 'weary for' means to long for.

notes.g: The world beyond death, or the open world outside.
notes.n: Catherine leaves it unclear, but she seems to mean freedom after death.

notes.t: incomparably beyond and above you all
notes.g: Far, far higher than all of you.

notes.m: Not 'unreasonable': here it means she seemed to have fainted.

notes.t: he gnashed at me, and foamed like a mad dog
notes.g: He snarled and frothed at me like a rabid dog.
notes.n: To 'gnash' is to grind your teeth in fury.

notes.t: a creature of my own species

notes.g: They'll wither you; they'll curse you.
notes.n: 'Blight' is a disease that withers plants.
Meant literally: Heathcliff says her betrayal of her own heart is a sin.

notes.t: the poor fancy you felt for Linton
notes.g: The feeble liking you had for Edgar.
notes.m: 'Fancy' here means a passing liking or attraction.

notes.n: An echo of Chapter IX, where Catherine said it would 'degrade' her to marry Heathcliff.

notes.m: 'Wasted' here means withered by illness, not squandered.

notes.t: I love my murderer—but yours! How can I?
notes.g: I can love you, who are killing me; but I can't love whoever is killing you.
notes.n: He means Catherine herself: by betraying her heart she has destroyed her own life, and that he cannot forgive.

notes.t: Heathcliff could weep on a great occasion like this
notes.g: Even Heathcliff could cry at a moment like this.

notes.t: the man whom I had sent off
notes.g: The servant she sent for oranges.

notes.t: a concourse thickening outside Gimmerton chapel porch
notes.g: A growing crowd outside the church entrance.
notes.n: A 'concourse' is a gathering of people. Church is letting out.

notes.g: The part of the house with the kitchen and servants' rooms.
Before you go to sleep tonight.
Heathcliff, who has entered without permission.
If he shot me like this, right here.

notes.t: I’d expire with a blessing on my lips
notes.n: To 'expire' is to breathe your last.

notes.t: she has not wit to help herself
notes.g: She hasn't the sense to look after herself.
I twisted my hands together in distress.
A load and a source of unhappiness.
Displays of feeling; any action he might take.
Catherine's body, looking as if dead.
Bring her round; wake her up.
Tall conifers that, unlike most, lose their needles in winter.

notes.t: delivered the house of his luckless presence
notes.g: Relieved the house of his ill-fated presence: he left.
